Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

let’s verb

also let us, let’s not, come on, let’s

classical

Ter. Eun. 459: Eāmus ergō ad cēnam
Hor. S. 1.1.27: āmōtō quaerāmus sēria lūdō

eāmus, videāmus

the present subjunctive, first person plural, in -āmus (-ēmus in the first conjugation); negative nē

let’s go, let’s see

Often after age or agite, “come on”. Negative nē: nē exspectēmus quidem, dum rogēmur, let’s not even wait to be asked.

Examples

  • Eāmus ergō ad cēnam: quid stās?

    Let’s go to dinner, then: why are you standing there?Ter. Eun. 459

  • Eāmus; dūc nōs, sōdēs.

    Let’s go; lead the way, please.Ter. Ph. 103

  • sed tamen āmōtō quaerāmus sēria lūdō

    but still, joking aside, let’s turn to serious thingsHor. S. 1.1.27

  • ergō vīvāmus, dum licet esse bene

    so let’s live, while we may have a good timePetr. 34.4

  • nē exspectēmus quidem, dum rogēmur; studium semper adsit, cūnctātiō absit

    let’s not even wait to be asked; let eagerness always be there and hesitation neverCic. Amic. 44

  • cantantēs licet ūsque (minus via laedit) eāmus

    let’s go singing all the way (the road hurts less)Verg. Ecl. 9.64

  • sed cum dīcitur, 'eāmus, faciāmus,' et pudet nōn esse impudentem

    but when someone says “let’s go, let’s do it”, one is ashamed not to be shamelessAug. Conf. 2.9.17

See also let, let’s keep going, shall.
